title: Maintenance Order
context: Plant Maintenance › Preventive & Breakdown Maintenance (PM) › Maintenance Order

cards.title: Where the Maintenance Order sits in the operational maintenance workflow
cards.body:
The Maintenance Order is step three in the preventive maintenance operational sequence.
It immediately follows the Maintenance Request where equipment faults are initially reported by operators.
Maintenance planners use this screen to translate a maintenance need into a detailed job plan.
It schedules required tasks, assigns responsible technicians, and plans replacement engineering spares.
The next operational step is issuing required replacement spares from warehouse stores to repair crews.
The order consolidates task instructions, safety permit check lists, and specialized tool requirements.
It serves as the binding authorization for technicians to perform physical repair work on plant machinery.
When work is completed, technicians report actual hours and equipment downtime against this order.
Accurate order planning ensures maintenance is executed safely, on time, and within approved budgets.
Authorizing the order releases material requisitions into warehouse management systems for stores fulfillment.
Without an authorized work order, storekeepers cannot issue spare parts for equipment overhauls.
This document provides complete traceability from initial fault detection to final operational sign-off.
Completed work orders provide baseline data for evaluating total maintenance expenditure by asset.
Operational managers review these transaction records periodically to verify adherence to organizational governance standards.

cards.title: Mandatory order headers, equipment selections, and location checks
cards.body:
Creating a maintenance order requires critical operational headers and asset selections in the system.
The user must select a valid reference object, target equipment, and maintenance category.
The operating division selected on the order must match the current physical location of the asset.
If the equipment location differs from the order division, the system immediately halts saving.
A valid maintenance type, source document, and responsible person must be recorded on the header.
The document date cannot precede the scheduled occurrence date of the maintenance job.
Estimated start dates cannot be earlier than the current document creation date.
Estimated end dates cannot precede the estimated start date under any operational circumstances.
Estimated job duration must be entered as a positive number of operating hours.
Missing mandatory headers halt saving and highlight the exact field requiring user attention on screen.
Division alignment rules ensure that repair expenditures are allocated to the correct operating facility.
Accurate header information establishes clear operational ownership and scheduling accountability.
Document dates prevent retroactive job scheduling and ensure chronological maintenance logging.
Operational managers review these transaction records periodically to verify adherence to organizational governance standards.

cards.title: Task scheduling constraints, fault assignments, and technician allocations
cards.body:
Every maintenance order must contain at least one valid maintenance task detail line in the schedule.
Assigned tasks must link to specific fault descriptions identified on the source maintenance request.
Task start dates cannot precede the overall estimated start date of the maintenance order.
Task completion dates cannot exceed the overall estimated end date of the maintenance order.
Resource allocations and technician assignments must align with scheduled task dates.
Technician service quantities cannot be left blank, zero, or negative on any allocation line.
Service items must possess valid billing rates and active maintenance skill classifications.
If breakdown status was flagged on the request, omitting breakdown flags triggers confirmation warnings.
These scheduling constraints ensure that tasks and resources fit realistically within the overhaul window.
Accurate task breakdown allows supervisors to monitor progress and track labor efficiency across jobs.
Predefined task sequences ensure that complex machinery overhauls follow standardized engineering protocols.
Proper resource alignment prevents scheduling conflicts among specialized maintenance technicians.
Resource planning ensures skilled labor is scheduled without causing overtime or factory downtime.
Operational managers review these transaction records periodically to verify adherence to organizational governance standards.

cards.title: Spares planning, warehouse requisitions, and material allocations
cards.body:
Planned replacement components must be specified on the item requirements section of the order.
Each spare line specifies the item reference, required quantity, unit, and designated warehouse.
Required spare quantities cannot be left blank, zero, or negative on any item line.
Spares selected must exist as active engineering inventory in Material Management masters.
Authorizing the maintenance order generates formal material requisitions for warehouse stores.
Storekeepers verify available stock and stage components prior to maintenance execution on site.
If required spares are out of stock, procurement indents are triggered automatically by the system.
Component consumption is charged directly to the equipment once items are issued by stores.
Accurate spares planning prevents job delays and minimizes unscheduled equipment downtime in the plant.
Technicians cannot withdraw unapproved spares without formal work order amendments.
This inventory integration guarantees complete material traceability and accurate machine maintenance costing.
Unused spare components must be formally returned to stores to credit the maintenance job.
Planned parts demands prevent delays by staging engineering components before shutdown overhauls begin.
Operational managers review these transaction records periodically to verify adherence to organizational governance standards.
Every milestone produces an auditable record connecting original requests to final authorized financial commitments.

cards.title: Work permit clearance, lockout tagout compliance, and safety sign-offs
cards.body:
When maintenance involves hazardous machinery, safety permit compliance is strictly mandatory.
Permit sections import required safety instructions and lockout tagout check lists from permit masters.
Technicians and safety officers must physically verify electrical and mechanical isolation on site.
If mandatory safety permits are unapproved, the system blocks starting the work order.
Safety check points must be signed off individually before machinery can be disassembled by technicians.
After work is finished, de-isolation procedures verify that tools and personnel are clear.
Work permits linked to the order must be formally surrendered upon job completion.
These safety controls prevent electrical shocks, toxic exposures, and machinery entrapment during overhauls.
Safety records remain permanently linked to the order for statutory occupational audits and compliance reviews.
Operating permits ensure that hazardous energy sources remain locked out until all technicians sign off.
This safety protocol protects human life and enforces strict industrial safety discipline.
Permit compliance prevents industrial accidents and protects technicians working in high-voltage areas.

cards.title: Authorization controls, record locking, and job completion sign-off
cards.body:
Maintenance orders advance through three formal operational statuses: Initial, Release, and Authorized.
Saving in Release status records the planner identity and queues the order for authorization review.
Under multi-tier authorization, only the final designated engineer can transition status to Authorized.
Attempting unauthorized status changes produces error notifications stopping the save operation in the system.
Once authorized, the maintenance order is completely locked against direct field modifications.
If work requirements change, an authorized maintenance order amendment must be created through formal channels.
When physical repairs conclude, technicians log actual hours, downtime, and return remaining spares.
Closing the order marks the job completed and releases the machinery back to operations.
Locked order records preserve an accurate history of maintenance interventions and repair costs.
Completed orders update equipment reliability metrics including mean time between failures.
This state progression guarantees strict managerial oversight over plant repair activities and maintenance budgets.
Historical work order data informs predictive maintenance algorithms and overhaul interval reviews.
Operational managers review these transaction records periodically to verify adherence to organizational governance standards.
Every milestone produces an auditable record connecting original requests to final authorized financial commitments.
